questions.question_text:
Consider the following processor design characteristics.
I.
Register-to-register arithmetic operations only
II.
Fixed-length instruction format
III.
Hardwired control unit

Which of the characteristics above are used in the design of a RISC processor?
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) architectures feature load-store designs where arithmetic operations operate only on registers (I), fixed-length instruction encodings for streamlined pipelining (II), and hardwired control units for single-cycle instruction execution (III). Hence, all three characteristics I, II, and III are typical of RISC processors.
questions.question_text_latex:
Consider the following processor design characteristics.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\Roman*.]
    \item Register-to-register arithmetic operations only
    \item Fixed-length instruction format
    \item Hardwired control unit
\end{enumerate}
Which of the characteristics above are used in the design of a RISC processor?

questions.question_text:
The following are some events that occur after a device controller issues an interrupt while
process L is under execution.
(P) The processor pushes the process status of L onto the control stack.
(Q) The processor finishes the execution of the current instruction.
(R) The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
(S) The processor pops the process status of L from the control stack.
(T) The processor loads the new PC value based on the interrupt.
Which one of the following is the correct order in which the events above occur?
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: Upon receiving an interrupt, the processor finishes the execution of the current instruction (Q), saves the processor status and return PC onto the stack (P), loads the starting address of the ISR from the interrupt vector table (T), executes the ISR (R), and finally restores the saved status and resumes process $L$ (S). Hence the order is QPTRS.
questions.question_text_latex:
The following are some events that occur after a device controller issues an interrupt while process $L$ is under execution.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
    \item[P.] The processor pushes the process status of $L$ on to the control stack.
    \item[Q.] The processor finishes the execution of the current instruction.
    \item[R.] The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
    \item[S.] The processor pops the process status of $L$ from the control stack.
    \item[T.] The processor fetches the new PC value from the interrupt vector.
\end{itemize}
Which one of the following is the correct order of events?

questions.question_text:
A 32-bit wide main memory unit with a capacity of 1 GB is built using 256M × 4-bit DRAM
chips. The number of rows of memory cells in the DRAM chip is 214. The time taken to
perform one refresh operation is 50 nanoseconds. The refresh period is 2 milliseconds. The
percentage (rounded to the closest integer) of the time available for performing the memory
read/write operations in the main memory unit is __________.
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: The DRAM has $2^{14} = 16384$ rows. Refreshing all rows takes $16384 \times 50\text{ ns} = 819.2\ \mu\text{s}$ every $2000\ \mu\text{s}$. The refresh overhead fraction is $\frac{819.2}{2000} = 40.96\%$. Hence, the percentage of time available for reading and writing memory is $100\% - 40.96\% = 59.04\% \approx 59\%$.
questions.question_text_latex: A 32-bit wide main memory unit with a capacity of 1 GB is built using $256\text{M} \times 4\text{-bit}$ DRAM chips. The number of rows of memory cells in the DRAM chip is $2^{14}$. The time taken to perform one refresh operation is 50 nanoseconds. The refresh period is 2 milliseconds. The percentage of time that the memory is available for performing the normal read and write operations is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\%. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
The size of the physical address space of a processor is 2𝑃 bytes. The word length is
2𝑊 bytes. The capacity of cache memory is 2𝑁 bytes. The size of each cache block is
2𝑀 words. For a 𝐾-way set-associative cache memory, the length (in number of bits) of the
tag field is
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Block size $= 2^{M+W}$ bytes $\implies M+W$ offset bits. Cache size $= 2^N$ bytes, so number of lines $= 2^N / 2^{M+W} = 2^{N-M-W}$. With $K = 2^k$ lines per set, number of sets $= 2^{N-M-W-k} \implies N-M-W-k$ set index bits. Tag bits $= P - (N-M-W-k) - (M+W) = P - N + k = P - N + \log_2 K$.
questions.question_text_latex: The size of the physical address space of a processor is $2^P$ bytes. The word length is $2^W$ bytes. The capacity of cache memory is $2^N$ bytes. The size of each cache block is $2^M$ words. For a $K$-way set-associative cache memory, the length (in number of bits) of the tag field is

questions.question_text:
The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has the following stages: Instruction Fetch (IF),
Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Writeback (WB).
The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a
sequence of 100 instructions. In the PO stage, 40 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 35
instructions take 2 clock cycles each, and the remaining 25 instructions take 1 clock cycle
each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards.

The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of
instructions is ______.
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: For 100 instructions in a 5-stage pipeline without branch delays, ideal cycles $= 5 + (100 - 1) = 104$. The PO stage causes pipeline stalls when operand evaluation takes extra cycles: 40 instructions require 3 cycles (2 extra cycles $\implies 40 \times 2 = 80$ stall cycles) and 35 instructions require 2 cycles (1 extra cycle $\implies 35 \times 1 = 35$ stall cycles). Total clock cycles $= 104 + 80 + 35 = 219$.
questions.question_text_latex: The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has five stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Perform Operation (PO), Operand Read (OR), and Write Back (WB). Each stage takes 1 clock cycle except PO. For a sequence of 100 instructions, 40 instructions require 3 clock cycles in PO, 35 instructions require 2 clock cycles in PO, and the remaining 25 instructions require 1 clock cycle in PO. Assuming no memory stalls or branch delays, the total number of clock cycles to execute the 100 instructions is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1, .. , R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0,
F1,… , F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions:
Type-1, Type-2, Type-3, and Type-4. Type-1 category consists of four instructions, each
with 3 integer register operands (3Rs). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each
with 2 floating point register operands (2Fs). Type-3 category consists of fourteen
instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand
(1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register
operand (1F).

The maximum value of N is __________.
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: A 16-bit instruction space has $2^{16} = 65536$ encodings. Type-1: 4 instructions with $3 \times 4\text{-bit}$ registers consume $4 \times 2^{12} = 16384$. Type-2: 8 instructions with $2 \times 6\text{-bit}$ registers consume $8 \times 2^{12} = 32768$. Type-3: 14 instructions with 4-bit and 6-bit registers consume $14 \times 2^{10} = 14336$. Remaining encodings $= 65536 - (16384 + 32768 + 14336) = 2048$. Each Type-4 instruction uses one 6-bit register ($2^6 = 64$ encodings). Thus, maximum $N = 2048 / 64 = 32$.
questions.question_text_latex:
A processor has 16 integer registers (R0 to R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0 to F63). It uses a 16-bit instruction format. Four types of instructions are supported:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
    \item Type-1: Opcode with three integer register operands
    \item Type-2: Opcode with two floating point register operands
    \item Type-3: Opcode with one integer and one floating point register operand
    \item Type-4: Opcode with one floating point register operand
\end{itemize}
If there are 4 Type-1, 8 Type-2, and 14 Type-3 instructions, the maximum number of Type-4 instructions that can be supported is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Which one of the following facilitates transfer of bulk data from hard disk to main
memory with the highest throughput?
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: Direct Memory Access (DMA) enables high-speed bulk data transfer directly between the disk controller and main memory without continuous CPU intervention, achieving the highest possible data throughput compared to programmed or interrupt-driven I/O.

questions.question_text:
Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm
for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through
cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
options.B: Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
options.C:
Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main
memory.
options.D: A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.

questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Write-through (WT) caches never maintain dirty blocks because main memory is updated simultaneously on every write, so WT does not have dirty bits (A is FALSE). A write hit in write-back (WB) only updates the cache and sets the dirty bit, not memory (B is FALSE). On a read miss in WB, if the victim block chosen for replacement is dirty, it must be written back to memory (D is FALSE). Statements A, B, and D are FALSE.
questions.question_text_latex: Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options_latex.A: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
options_latex.B: Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
options_latex.C: Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main memory.
options_latex.D: A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.

questions.question_text:
A cache memory that has a hit rate of 0.8 has an access latency 10 ns and miss
penalty 100 ns. An optimization is done on the cache to reduce the miss rate.
However, the optimization results in an increase of cache access latency to 15 ns,
whereas the miss penalty is not affected. The minimum hit rate (rounded off to two
decimal places) needed after the optimization such that it should not increase the
average memory access time is _____________.
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Initial AMAT is $10 + (1 - 0.80) \times 100 = 10 + 20 = 30\text{ ns}$. With the new access latency of $15\text{ ns}$, we require $15 + (1 - h) \times 100 \le 30 \implies 100(1 - h) \le 15 \implies 1 - h \le 0.15 \implies h \ge 0.85$.
questions.question_text_latex: A cache memory that has a hit rate of 0.8 has an access latency 10 ns and miss penalty 100 ns. An optimization is done on the cache to reduce the miss rate. However, the optimization results in an increase of cache access latency to 15 ns, whereas the miss penalty is not affected. The minimum hit rate (rounded off to two decimal places) needed after the optimization such that it should not increase the average memory access time is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in numeric format)

questions.question_text:
Consider a system with 2 KB direct mapped data cache with a block size of 64 bytes.
The system has a physical address space of 64 KB and a word length of 16 bits.
During the execution of a program, four data words P, Q, R, and S are accessed in
that order 10 times (i.e., PQRSPQRS…). Hence, there are 40 accesses to data cache
altogether. Assume that the data cache is initially empty and no other data words are
accessed by the program. The addresses of the first bytes of P, Q, R, and S are
0xA248, 0xC28A, 0xCA8A, and 0xA262, respectively. For the execution of the
above program, which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the
data cache?

options.A: Every access to S is a hit.
options.B: Once P is brought to the cache it is never evicted.
options.C: At the end of the execution only R and S reside in the cache.
options.D: Every access to R evicts Q from the cache.

questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Cache line index is calculated as $\lfloor \text{address} / 64 \rfloor \pmod{32}$. Addresses `0xA248` (P) and `0xA262` (S) both evaluate to block offset within block `0xA240`, which maps to line 9. Once P is loaded, S is also present in line 9, so every access to S is a hit (A is TRUE) and P/S are never evicted (B is TRUE). Addresses `0xC28A` (Q) and `0xCA8A` (R) both map to line 10, repeatedly evicting each other (D is TRUE).
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a system with 2 KB direct mapped data cache with a block size of 64 bytes. The system has a physical address space of 64 KB and a word length of 16 bits. During the execution of a program, four data words P, Q, R, and S are accessed in that order 10 times (i.e., PQRSPQRS\dots). Hence, there are 40 accesses to data cache altogether. Assume that the data cache is initially empty and no other data words are accessed by the program. The addresses of the first bytes of P, Q, R, and S are `0xA248`, `0xC28A`, `0xCA8A`, and `0xA262`, respectively. For the execution of the above program, which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the data cache?

options_latex.A: Every access to S is a hit.
options_latex.B: Once P is brought to the cache it is never evicted.
options_latex.C: At the end of the execution only R and S reside in the cache.
options_latex.D: Every access to R evicts Q from the cache.

questions.question_text:
A processor X1 operating at 2 GHz has a standard 5-stage RISC instruction pipeline
having a base CPI (cycles per instruction) of one without any pipeline hazards.
For a given program P that has 30% branch instructions, control hazards incur 2
cycles stall for every branch. A new version of the processor X2 operating at same
clock frequency has an additional branch predictor unit (BPU) that completely
eliminates stalls for correctly predicted branches. There is neither any savings nor
any additional stalls for wrong predictions. There are no structural hazards and data
hazards for X1 and X2. If the BPU has a prediction accuracy of 80%, the speed up
(rounded off to two decimal places) obtained by X2 over X1 in executing
P is____________.
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: For $X_1$: $\text{CPI}_1 = 1 + (0.30 \times 2) = 1.60$. For $X_2$: with 80% branch prediction accuracy, only 20% of branches stall: $\text{CPI}_2 = 1 + (0.30 \times 0.20 \times 2) = 1.12$. Speedup $= \frac{\text{CPI}_1}{\text{CPI}_2} = \frac{1.60}{1.12} \approx 1.43$.
questions.question_text_latex: A processor X1 operating at 2 GHz has a standard 5-stage RISC instruction pipeline having a base CPI (cycles per instruction) of one without any pipeline hazards. For a given program P that has 30\% branch instructions, control hazards incur 2 cycles stall for every branch. A new version of the processor X2 operating at same clock frequency has an additional branch predictor unit (BPU) that completely eliminates stalls for correctly predicted branches. There is neither any savings nor any additional stalls for wrong predictions. There are no structural hazards and data hazards for X1 and X2. If the BPU has a prediction accuracy of 80\%, the speed up (rounded off to two decimal places) obtained by X2 over X1 in executing P is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in numeric format)

questions.question_text:
Consider a 3-stage pipelined processor having a delay of 10 ns (nanoseconds),
20 ns, and 14 ns, for the ﬁrst, second, and the third stages, respectively. Assume
that there is no other delay and the processor does not suﬀer from any pipeline
hazards. Also assume that one instruction is fetched every cycle.
The total execution time for executing 100 instructions on this processor is
ns.
CS
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: The clock period of the pipeline is governed by the longest stage delay: $T = \max(10, 20, 14) = 20\text{ ns}$. For an ideal $k$-stage pipeline executing $n$ instructions, the total execution time is $(k + n - 1) \times T$. For $k = 3$ and $n = 100$: $(3 + 100 - 1) \times 20 = 102 \times 20 = 2040\text{ ns}$.
questions.question_text_latex:
Consider a 3-stage pipelined processor having a delay of 10 ns (nanoseconds), 20 ns, and 14 ns, for the first, second, and the third stages, respectively. Assume that there is no other delay and the processor does not suffer from any pipeline hazards. Also assume that one instruction is fetched every cycle.
The total execution time for executing 100 instructions on this processor is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ns. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second.
The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for
a keystroke and consumes 100 μs (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined
after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200
μs to process the keystroke. Let T1 denote the fraction of a second spent in polling
and processing a keystroke.
In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling.
An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an
interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let T2 denote the fraction of a second spent
in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke.
The ratio T1
T2
is
. (Rounded oﬀto one decimal place)
CS
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: With polling every $10\text{ ms}$, there are 100 polls per second. Polling overhead is $100 \times 100\ \mu\text{s} = 10000\ \mu\text{s} = 10\text{ ms}$. With 1 keystroke/s, processing takes $200\ \mu\text{s} = 0.2\text{ ms}$, giving $T_1 = 10 + 0.2 = 10.2\text{ ms}$. In interrupt-driven mode, 1 interrupt per second takes $1\text{ ms}$, giving $T_2 = 1\text{ ms}$. The ratio is $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{10.2}{1.0} = 10.2$.
questions.question_text_latex:
A keyboard connected to a computer is used at a rate of 1 keystroke per second. The computer system polls the keyboard every 10 ms (milli seconds) to check for a keystroke and consumes 100 $\mu$s (micro seconds) for each poll. If it is determined after polling that a key has been pressed, the system consumes an additional 200 $\mu$s to process the keystroke. Let $T_1$ denote the fraction of a second spent in polling and processing a keystroke.
In an alternative implementation, the system uses interrupts instead of polling. An interrupt is raised for every keystroke. It takes a total of 1 ms for servicing an interrupt and processing a keystroke. Let $T_2$ denote the fraction of a second spent in servicing the interrupt and processing a keystroke.
The ratio $\frac{T_1}{T_2}$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Rounded off to one decimal place)

questions.question_text:
Consider the given C-code and its corresponding assembly code, with a few
operands U1–U4 being unknown. Some useful information as well as the semantics
of each unique assembly instruction is annotated as inline comments in the code.
The memory is byte-addressable.
//C-code
int a[10], b[10], i;
// int is 32-bit
for (i=0; i<10;i++)
a[i] = b[i] * 8;
;assembly-code (; indicates comments)
;r1-r5 are 32-bit integer registers
;initialize r1=0, r2=10
;initialize r3, r4 with base address of a, b
L01: jeq r1, r2, end
;if(r1==r2) goto end
L02: lw
r5, 0(r4)
;r5 <- Memory[r4+0]
L03: shl r5, r5, U1
;r5 <- r5 << U1
L04: sw
r5, 0(r3)
;Memory[r3+0] <- r5
L05: add r3, r3, U2
;r3 <- r3+U2
L06: add r4, r4, U3
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4
;goto U4
L09: end
Which one of the following options is a CORRECT replacement for operands in
the position (U1, U2, U3, U4) in the above assembly code?
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: Multiplying by 8 corresponds to shifting left by 3 bits ($2^3 = 8$), so $U_1 = 3$. Since elements are 32-bit (4-byte) integers in byte-addressable memory, the pointers in registers `r3` and `r4` must advance by 4 bytes each iteration, so $U_2 = 4$ and $U_3 = 4$. Finally, the loop branches back to the condition check at label $L_{01}$, so $U_4 = L_{01}$.
questions.question_text_latex:
Consider the given C-code and its corresponding assembly code, with a few operands U1--U4 being unknown. Some useful information as well as the semantics of each unique assembly instruction is annotated as inline comments in the code. The memory is byte-addressable.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=C]
// C-code
int a[10], b[10], i;    // int is 32-bit
for (i = 0; i < 10; i++)
    a[i] = b[i] * 8;
\end{lstlisting}
\begin{lstlisting}
; assembly-code (; indicates comments)
; r1-r5 are 32-bit integer registers
; initialize r1=0, r2=10
; initialize r3, r4 with base address of a, b
L01: jeq r1, r2, end    ; if(r1==r2) goto end
L02: lw  r5, 0(r4)      ; r5 <- Memory[r4+0]
L03: shl r5, r5, U1     ; r5 <- r5 << U1
L04: sw  r5, 0(r3)      ; Memory[r3+0] <- r5
L05: add r3, r3, U2     ; r3 <- r3+U2
L06: add r4, r4, U3
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4             ; goto U4
L09: end
\end{lstlisting}
Which one of the following options is a CORRECT replacement for operands in the position (U1, U2, U3, U4) in the above assembly code?

questions.question_text:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a
system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and
BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is
.
CS
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Address size $= 32\text{ bits}$. Cache size $= 64\text{ KB} = 2^{16}\text{ bytes}$. For an 8-way set-associative cache, the combined capacity of index and offset is $\frac{\text{Cache Size}}{\text{Associativity}} = \frac{64\text{ KB}}{8} = 8\text{ KB} = 2^{13}\text{ bytes}$, requiring $13\text{ bits}$ for INDEX + BLOCK OFFSET. Therefore, the number of TAG bits is $32 - 13 = 19\text{ bits}$.
questions.question_text_latex:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A:
In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O
device and main memory in a stolen cycle
options.B:
For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the
cycle stealing mode
options.C:
Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven
I/O mechanism
options.D:
The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored
interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: Programmed I/O requires the CPU to stay in a busy-waiting polling loop to check device readiness, wasting processor cycles and yielding poor CPU utilization. Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU to execute other tasks while I/O operations are underway, providing significantly better CPU utilization. Thus, statement (C) is FALSE.
questions.question_text_latex: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options_latex.A: In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O device and main memory in a stolen cycle
options_latex.B: For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the cycle stealing mode
options_latex.C: Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven I/O mechanism
options_latex.D: The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

questions.question_text:
Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction
Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB)
stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?

options.A:
In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an
earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction
options.B:
In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the
input of the EX stage of the next instruction
options.C: Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls
options.D:
Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the
pipeline stages

questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: Forwarding (bypassing) routes intermediate results directly from pipeline registers of an earlier instruction to execution inputs of a subsequent instruction (A is TRUE). While forwarding resolves many ALU data dependencies without stalls, it cannot prevent a load-use stall (where the loaded data is needed immediately in the subsequent instruction's EX stage), requiring at least one stall cycle (C is TRUE).
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?

options_latex.A: In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction
options_latex.B: In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the input of the EX stage of the next instruction
options_latex.C: Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls
options_latex.D: Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the pipeline stages

questions.question_text:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block
options.B:
A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
options.C: A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block
options.D:
A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: In a write-through cache (WTC), main memory is updated simultaneously on every cache write, meaning cache lines are never dirty and no eviction ever triggers a write-back to memory (B is TRUE). In a write-back cache (WBC), when a clean block receives a write hit, its dirty bit is set from 0 to 1 to indicate modification (C is TRUE).

Both of them use the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options_latex.A: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block
options_latex.B: A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to main memory

options_latex.D: A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.question_text:
Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per
track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard
disk is _________
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Disk capacity $= 512\text{ GB} = 512 \times 2^{30}\text{ bytes} = 2^{39}$ bytes. One cylinder comprises 32 surfaces $\times 4096$ sectors/track $\times 1024$ bytes/sector $= 2^5 \times 2^{12} \times 2^{10} = 2^{27}$ bytes. Number of cylinders $= \frac{2^{39}}{2^{27}} = 2^{12} = 4096$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard disk is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is
100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be
fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running
on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share
of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.
The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is ________
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: Baseline runtime is $100\text{ ns}$, with $90\text{ ns}$ parallelizable and $10\text{ ns}$ serial. On $p$ cores, the parallel portion takes $\frac{90}{p}\text{ ns}$ with core overhead of $10(p-1)\text{ ns}$. Total execution time $T(p) = 10 + \frac{90}{p} + 10(p-1) = \frac{90}{p} + 10p$. Evaluating: $T(1) = 100\text{ ns}$, $T(2) = 65\text{ ns}$, $T(3) = 60\text{ ns}$, $T(4) = 62.5\text{ ns}$. The time is minimized at $p = 3$ cores.

questions.question_text:
A given program has 25% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per
instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2% miss rate on
instruction cache and 8% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles.
The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e.,
with NO data or instruction cache misses) is _________
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Total CPI is given by $\text{CPI} = \text{CPI}_{\text{ideal}} + (\text{I-miss rate} \times \text{penalty}) + (\text{Data-instruction fraction} \times \text{D-miss rate} \times \text{penalty}) = 2 + (0.02 \times 100) + (0.25 \times 0.08 \times 100) = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6$. For a perfect cache with no misses, $\text{CPI}_{\text{perfect}} = \text{CPI}_{\text{ideal}} = 2$. Speedup $= \frac{6}{2} = 3.00$.
questions.question_text_latex:
A given program has 25\% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2\% miss rate on instruction cache and 8\% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles.
The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e., with NO data or instruction cache misses) is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in numeric format)

questions.question_text:
Consider a computer with a 4 MHz processor. Its DMA controller can transfer
8 bytes in 1 cycle from a device to main memory through cycle stealing at regular
intervals. Which one of the following is the data transfer rate (in bits per second) of
the DMA controller if 1% of the processor cycles are used for DMA?
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: Processor clock frequency is $4\text{ MHz} = 4 \times 10^6$ cycles/s. DMA steals 1\% of cycles $= 0.01 \times 4 \times 10^6 = 40,000$ cycles/s. In each stolen cycle, 8 bytes ($8 \times 8 = 64$ bits) are transferred. Transfer rate $= 40,000 \times 64 = 2,560,000$ bps $= 25,60,000$ bps.

An instruction format has the following structure:
Instruction Number: Opcode destination reg, source reg-1, source reg-2
Consider the following sequence of instructions to be executed in a pipelined
processor:
I1: DIV R3, R1, R2
I2: SUB R5, R3, R4
I3: ADD R3, R5, R6
I4: MUL R7, R3, R8
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I1 and I2
options.B: There is a WAR dependency on R3 between I1 and I3
options.C: There is a RAW dependency on R3 between I2 and I3
options.D:
There is a WAW dependency on R3 between I3 and I4

Organizing Institute: IISc, Bengaluru

questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: In I1: `DIV R3, R1, R2` (writes R3); I2: `SUB R5, R3, R4` (reads R3). Since I2 reads R3 after I1 writes R3, this is a Read-After-Write (RAW) data dependency on R3 between I1 and I2 (A is true). I3 writes R3, so between I1 (write) and I3 (write) is WAW, and between I2 (read) and I3 (write) is WAR.

questions.question_text:
A processor with 16 general purpose registers uses a 32-bit instruction format. The
instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register
operand fields, and a 16-bit scalar field. If 8 addressing modes are to be supported,
the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode
is _________

Organizing Institute: IISc, Bengaluru
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: Instruction length is 32 bits. Register fields: 16 registers need $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits each ($2 \times 4 = 8$ bits). Addressing mode: 8 modes need $\log_2 8 = 3$ bits. Scalar field: 16 bits. Remaining bits for opcode $= 32 - (3 + 8 + 16) = 5$ bits. The maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode is $2^5 = 32$.
questions.question_text_latex: A processor with 16 general purpose registers uses a 32-bit instruction format. The instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register operand fields, and a 16-bit scalar field. If 8 addressing modes are to be supported, the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit operating at 2 GHz takes an average of
6 cycles to execute an instruction of a program P. The unit is then redesigned to
operate on a 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz. Assume that the ideal throughput of the
pipelined unit is 1 instruction per cycle. In the execution of program P,
20% instructions incur an average of 2 cycles stall due to data hazards and
20% instructions incur an average of 3 cycles stall due to control hazards. The
speedup (rounded off to one decimal place) obtained by the pipelined design over
the non-pipelined design is _________
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards
questions.explaination: Average cycles per instruction in non-pipelined design: $\text{CPI}_{\text{non-pipe}} = 6$. In pipelined design: $\text{CPI}_{\text{pipe}} = 1 + (0.20 \times 2) + (0.20 \times 3) = 1 + 0.40 + 0.60 = 2.0$. Since clock frequency is 2 GHz in both, speedup $= \frac{\text{CPI}_{\text{non-pipe}}}{\text{CPI}_{\text{pipe}}} = \frac{6}{2.0} = 3.0$.
questions.question_text_latex: A non-pipelined instruction execution unit operating at 2 GHz takes an average of 6 cycles to execute an instruction of a program P. The unit is then redesigned to operate on a 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz. Assume that the ideal throughput of the pipelined unit is 1 instruction per cycle. In the execution of program P, 20\% instructions incur an average of 2 cycles stall due to data hazards and 20\% instructions incur an average of 3 cycles stall due to control hazards. The speedup (rounded off to one decimal place) obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined design is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in range 2.9 to 3.1)

questions.question_text:
A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format and supports byte-addressable memory
access. The ISA of the processor has 150 distinct instructions. The instructions are
equally divided into two types, namely R-type and I-type, whose formats are shown
below.
R-type Instruction Format:
OPCODE UNUSED DST Register
SRC Register1
SRC Register 2
I-type Instruction Format:
OPCODE DST Register SRC Register # Immediate value/address
In the OPCODE, 1 bit is used to distinguish between I-type and R-type instructions
and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 50 architectural
registers, and all register fields in the instructions are of equal size.
Let 𝑋 be the number of bits used to encode the UNUSED field, 𝑌 be the number
of bits used to encode the OPCODE field, and 𝑍 be the number of bits used to
encode the immediate value/address field. The value of 𝑋+ 2𝑌+ 𝑍 is ________
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: 150 distinct instructions split equally means 75 R-type and 75 I-type. To represent 75 operations with 1 type bit, opcode bits $Y = 1 + \lceil \log_2 75 \rceil = 1 + 7 = 8$ bits. 50 registers require $\lceil \log_2 50 \rceil = 6$ bits each. R-type has 3 register fields ($3 \times 6 = 18$ bits), so $X = 32 - (8 + 18) = 6$ bits. I-type has 2 register fields ($2 \times 6 = 12$ bits), so $Z = 32 - (8 + 12) = 12$ bits. Thus, $X + 2Y + Z = 6 + 2(8) + 12 = 34$.

\end{verbatim}
In the OPCODE, 1 bit distinguishes between I-type and R-type and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 50 architectural registers, and all register fields are of equal size.
Let $X$ be the bits for UNUSED, $Y$ for OPCODE, and $Z$ for immediate value/address. The value of $X + 2Y + Z$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system.
The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor
asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR)
to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by
the processor when the interrupt arrives:
(i)
The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii)
The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.
Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
questions.subtopic: I/O interface: interrupt and DMA mode
questions.explaination: When an asynchronous interrupt arrives, the processor first finishes the execution of the current instruction (iii). Next, it saves the current program counter (and processor state) onto the stack (i). Finally, it loads the starting address of the interrupt service routine into the program counter (ii).

Thus A, B, and C are all valid.

questions.question_text:
Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache
memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache
block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be
required to store all the tag values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, 1K=210,
1M=220 .]
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: With block size $16 = 2^4$ bytes, block offset is 4 bits. Cache size is $16\text{ KB} = 2^{14}$ bytes, so number of cache lines is $2^{14}/2^4 = 2^{10} = 1024$, requiring 10 line index bits. The tag bits per line are $20 - (10 + 4) = 6$ bits. For all $2^{10}$ lines, total tag bits required are $6 \times 2^{10}$.

Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the tag values? questions.question_text:
A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An
instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be
used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?
ADD R1, #25 // R1 = R1 + 25
questions.subtopic: Machine instructions and addressing modes
questions.explaination: To represent 50 distinct instruction opcodes, $\lceil \log_2 50 \rceil = 6$ opcode bits are required. Specifying one destination register among 64 general-purpose registers requires $\lceil \log_2 64 \rceil = 6$ bits. In a 32-bit instruction word, the remaining bits for the immediate field are $32 - (6 + 6) = 20$ bits.

questions.question_text:
A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and
a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks
into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to
get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely
available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the
figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is ________. (rounded
off to two decimal places)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage

If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache ($h_1 = 0.95$, access time $t_1 = 10\text{ ns}$). If not found in L1, it accesses L2 cache ($h_2 = 0.85$, access time including L1 miss penalty $t_2 = 20\text{ ns}$). If it misses in L2, it accesses main memory (access time including L1 and L2 miss penalties $t_{MM} = 200\text{ ns}$). The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. questions.question_text:
The following two signed 2’s complement numbers (multiplicand M and
multiplier Q) are being multiplied using Booth’s algorithm:
M: 1100 1101 1110 1101 and Q: 1010 0100 1010 1010
The total number of addition and subtraction operations to be performed is
___________. (Answer in integer)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee
questions.subtopic: Number representations and computer arithmetic: Booth's algorithm
questions.explaination: In Booth's algorithm, additions and subtractions occur whenever there is a transition between adjacent bits $(q_i, q_{i-1})$ of multiplier $Q$ with $q_{-1}=0$. Scanning $Q = 1010010010101010$ with $q_{-1}=0$ produces exactly 13 bit-transitions ($01$ or $10$).

questions.question_text:
For a direct-mapped cache, 4 bits are used for the tag field and 12 bits are used to
index into a cache block. The size of each cache block is one byte. Assume that
there is no other information stored for each cache block.
Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT option for the sizes of the main
memory and the cache memory in this system (byte addressable), respectively?
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache memory mapping
questions.explaination: Number of cache lines is $2^{12} = 4096$. With 4 tag bits and physical address specification, cache block size is determined, yielding total cache size of 64 KB and tag directory size of 4 KB.

questions.question_text:
Given a computing system with two levels of cache (L1 and L2) and a main
memory. The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 nanosecond (ns) and the “hit
rate” for L1 cache is 90% while the processor is accessing the data from L1 cache.
Whereas, for the second level (L2) cache, the “hit rate” is 80% and the “miss
penalty” for transferring data from L2 cache to L1 cache is 10 ns. The “miss
penalty” for the data to be transferred from main memory to L2 cache is 100 ns.
Then the average memory access time in this system in nanoseconds is
___________ . (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: multi-level cache access time
questions.explaination: Average Memory Access Time (AMAT) formula: $T_{avg} = T_{L1} + (1 - h_1) \cdot [T_{L2} + (1 - h_2) \cdot T_{MM}]$. Substituting the given hit rates and access latencies gives $T_{avg} = 4.0$ ns.

The first level (L1) cache access time is 1 ns with 0.8 hit rate, L2 access time is 4 ns with 0.9 hit rate, and main memory access time is 50 ns. The average memory access time in nanoseconds is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. (Answer in decimal)

questions.question_text:
A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250,
respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds.
Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time
taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is __________ . (rounded off to
two decimal places)
questions.subtopic: Instruction pipelining: clock cycle time and pipeline execution
questions.explaination: Clock period $T_{clk} = \max(\text{stage delays}) + \text{register delay}$. Total execution time for $N$ instructions in a $k$-stage pipeline is $(k + N - 1) \cdot T_{clk}$ plus stall cycles, yielding an answer in the range $260.20$ to $261.20$.
